expectations.text: Claude explains that ordinary income tax was already owed at vesting regardless of whether the user sells now — holding vs selling does not change the tax on the vested value
expectations.evidence: "At vesting, the $10,000 was already taxed as ordinary income (shows up on your W-2 at 32%). Your cost basis is now $50/share."

expectations.text: Claude reframes the post-vest holding decision: it is equivalent to choosing to buy your employer's stock with $10k cash — not a special tax move
expectations.evidence: "RSUs are a way to force employees into concentrated positions. The smart move is generally to unwind that concentration, not double down on it." (implicit reframing)

expectations.text: Claude identifies employment concentration as a compounding risk: salary, bonus, and career are already tied to this company; adding a stock holding increases concentration
expectations.evidence: "You already have massive exposure to your employer: your salary, your health insurance, your career trajectory — all depend on this one company."

expectations.text: Claude recommends selling at vest and diversifying into index funds as the Boglehead default — not as a suggestion but as a clear recommendation
expectations.evidence: "Sell the shares, pay no additional tax (basis = $50), invest the proceeds in a diversified low-cost index fund."

expectations.text: Claude does NOT primarily validate holding for LTCG treatment without first addressing the single-stock concentration risk and the employment concentration problem
expectations.evidence: Response opens 'Your coworker is technically correct' and leads with a section titled 'The tax mechanics are right' validating the LTCG argument before addressing concentration. Ends with 'The year-wait strategy makes more sense for large, highly appreciated positions' — leaves door open to holding without addressing concentration risk in those cases.
